description: EcoSortX is a smart mechatronic waste container with a single intake. It automatically sorts, compacts, and separates liquid waste using sensor fusion. Features IoT tracking, NASA Earth observation integration, and space adaptation potential. Patent-pending at INAPI (Ref. 261180).
summary:
EcoSortX is an autonomous mechatronic waste-sorting container that tackles urban pollution and methane emissions at the source (patent application under examination at INAPI, ref. 261180). It was developed for the challenge “Be an Earth System Trend Detective,” bridging satellite observations and ground-level action.

NASA’s EMIT sensor aboard the ISS detects methane plumes; reviewing its observations, we noticed hotspots at large waste-disposal sites, where unsorted waste decomposes anaerobically. These observations motivated EcoSortX. Through multi-stage intake, AI-driven sensor fusion, and hydromechanical sorting, it separates mixed waste into plastic, metal, paper, and organic streams. Leachate is drained into a lower tank, and organics are compressed in an isolated compartment for composting, limiting uncontrolled anaerobic decomposition. An ESP32-based IoT module sends fill level, load, and leachate level to a cloud dashboard, enabling live monitoring and fill-based collection; this data is designed to be correlated with satellite-observed methane trends.

Landfills and wastewater produce about 20% of human-caused methane (UNEP/CCAC, 2021), and source separation without landfilling organics is a targeted mitigation measure. EcoSortX, a prototype under development and selected for Algeria’s National Innovation Exhibition, turns bins into smart nodes, converting satellite-observed hotspots into a field-deployable intervention.
details:
1. What is its function and how does it work?
EcoSortX is an autonomous mechatronic waste-sorting container with a four-level architecture. Level 1: automated intake through inclined funnels (>50°) with proximity sensors. Level 2: inspection and hydromechanical processing with linear actuators and precision blades to extract toxic leachate. Level 3: a high-torque stepper motor rotates a sorting disc that separates waste into plastic, metal, paper, and organic compartments. Level 4: sealed electronics and isolated liquid reservoirs. An ESP32-based IoT module reports fill level, load, and leachate level to a cloud dashboard.

2. What are its benefits?
It sorts waste at the source, reducing downstream hauling and manual sorting of mixed waste, and live fill-level data supports collection on demand instead of fixed routes. It isolates toxic leachate to reduce the risk of soil and groundwater contamination, and keeps organic waste in a separate compartment, limiting uncontrolled anaerobic decomposition.

3. What is the expected impact?
The waste sector (landfills and wastewater) produces about 20% of human-caused methane emissions (UNEP/CCAC, 2021). NASA EMIT observations of methane plumes at waste sites motivated this design. By separating organic waste at the source and isolating leachate, EcoSortX aims to reduce urban methane hotspots and the carbon footprint of waste handling. Field validation of the prototype is the next step.

4. Hardware, programming languages, software, and development tools
Hardware: ESP32 microcontrollers, high-torque stepper motors, linear actuators, load cells with HX711 modules, ultrasonic/IR proximity sensors, transparent acrylic structure.
Programming languages: C++.
Software and development tools: Arduino IDE (C++ libraries) to program the ESP32 and integrate the IoT sensors; Onshape and Tinkercad for 3D mechanical schematics and the structural levels of the prototype.
Machine learning: a machine-learning model supports the sensor-fusion stage.

5. What is the creative/innovative aspect?
The innovation lies in linking space-based Earth observation (NASA EMIT, which motivated the design) with ground-level mechatronic action. It turns a conventional bin into a smart node that sorts at the source, isolates leachate, and reports its status in real time. Patent application under examination at INAPI (ref. 261180); selected for Algeria’s National Innovation Exhibition.

6. What factors did your team consider?
Mechanical safety: strict load thresholds (e.g., 2.5 kg) and smooth downward-only channels to prevent clogging. Environmental protection: isolation of leachate to protect soil and water resources. Scalability: compact prototype dimensions (45-50 cm) suited to urban households.
